text.title: Alert-to-Fix Incident Loop Core Rules
text.summary: 7 testable rules binding the solo on-call loop — alert → triage → mitigate → fix → postmortem → alert-quality patch. Each rule is checkable against the alerting rule file, the incident record's timestamps, or the ticket tracker.

rule.statement: For sev1 and sev2 the first recorded action MUST be a service-restoring one — roll back the last deploy, flip the feature flag off, shift traffic, scale out — and `mitigation` carries its own timestamp, distinct from the `root_cause` entry. Diagnosis continues after the bleeding stops.
rule.rationale: Time-to-mitigate and time-to-diagnose are independent; a rollback is available in minutes while a root cause routinely takes hours. Responders who chase the cause first spend the entire customer-impact window in a debugger, and the impact figure in the postmortem is then a measure of curiosity, not of the fault.

rule.statement: A rule with paging severity MUST fire on a user-visible symptom or on SLO error-budget burn rate — e.g. multiwindow multi-burn-rate: 14.4x burn sustained over 1h (2% of a 30-day budget) pages, 6x over 6h pages, 1x over 3d tickets. Cause metrics (CPU, memory, queue depth, pod restarts, disk IOPS) MUST route to ticket or dashboard severity, never to a page.

rationale.source: Google SRE Workbook, ch. 5 "Alerting on SLOs"

rule.rationale: Cause alerts fire on states the system routinely survives — a saturated CPU with the SLO intact is a page with nothing to do. The multiwindow form exists because a single short window pages on transients and a single long window is slow to notice a fast burn; the pair gives both precision and detection time.

rule.statement: Every paging rule MUST carry a `runbook_url` annotation (Prometheus `annotations.runbook_url`, or the equivalent field in the alerting backend) resolving to a page that opens with the first three commands or dashboard links to run. A page that fires without one is an alert-quality defect, and `alert_quality_patch` for that incident is the annotation plus the runbook page.

rationale.source: Google SRE Book, ch. 11 "Being On-Call" — playbooks report roughly a 3x MTTR improvement

rule.rationale: Most of a solo responder's first fifteen minutes goes to rediscovery: which dashboard, which service, what the last similar page was. The runbook converts that from recall under adrenaline to a click, which is why its measured effect is on MTTR rather than on correctness.

rule.statement: Closing an incident requires marking the page `actionable` or `not-actionable` and recomputing the rolling actionability rate (actionable pages / total pages over the trailing window). When the rate falls below the stated threshold, the next `alert_quality_patch` MUST change the rule — add a `for:` hold-down, move to burn rate, narrow the label selector, add an inhibition or a maintenance-window silence — rather than documenting another response.

rationale.source: Google SRE Book, ch. 11 — a page must be actionable, novel and urgent; on-call load target of no more than ~2 incidents per 12-hour shift

rule.rationale: Noise is measured per rule but felt per responder: once a fraction of pages are known non-events, the responder starts triaging by intuition and the true positive that arrives at 03:00 is dismissed with the same reflex as the last five false ones.

rule.statement: An alert that fires and self-resolves inside its own evaluation window MUST be fixed with a duration hold-down (`for: 10m`), a longer averaging window, or a burn-rate formulation — not by raising the static threshold. Check: the patch diff touches `for:`/window, not only the comparison constant.

rationale.source: Prometheus alerting-rule semantics (`for` clause) and the SRE Workbook's precision/recall framing

rule.rationale: Raising the threshold trades recall for precision uniformly: the flapping stops and so does detection of the slower, larger version of the same fault. A hold-down discards only transients whose duration is below the one the SLO cares about, which is the distinction the threshold cannot express.

rule.statement: Every postmortem action item MUST exist as a filed ticket with a single named human owner and a due date, and the postmortem links the ticket ids. A recommendation that appears only as a sentence in the document is not an action item and does not close the loop.
rule.rationale: Items that live only in the document have no queue that surfaces them and no owner whose backlog shows them, so they are reread only during the next postmortem for the same failure. Ticketing is what makes the follow-up visible in the place the operator actually looks each morning.

rule.statement: Do NOT run the loop when (a) the alert is a known false positive already scheduled for muting — file the mute and stop; (b) the incident spans several teams or vendors and needs a coordinated incident commander with a comms lead, which this solo loop does not model; (c) there is no alerting rule at all and the incident was reported by a customer — first close the detection gap, since there is no `alert_id` to patch.

rationale.source: Methodology preconditions + SRE incident-command role separation

rule.rationale: The loop's closing step patches an alerting rule; with no rule to patch, or with the response split across people the record has no field for, the artefact ends up complete-looking and structurally empty, which is worse than an explicit skip.
